column2:
• == has a special rule for null and undefined.
  • It returns true when one side is null and the other is undefined.
  • Neither value is converted.
null == undefined // true

• === does not use the special loose-equality rule.
  • null and undefined are different JavaScript language types.
  • Different types return false.
  • typeof null reports "object" because of a historical JavaScript behavior.
null === undefined // false

• JavaScript sees a number and a string.
  • Loose equality converts the string to a number.
  • "5" becomes 5.
  • JavaScript compares 5 == 5.
5 == "5" // true

• JavaScript sees a number and a boolean.
  • Loose equality converts false to 0.
  • JavaScript compares 0 == 0.
0 == false // true

• An empty array is an object.
  • JavaScript converts [] to the empty string "".
  • JavaScript converts "" to the number 0.
  • JavaScript compares 0 == 0.
[] == 0 // true

• An empty object is an object.
  • JavaScript converts {} to "[object Object]".
  • "[object Object]" cannot become a number.
  • JavaScript gets NaN.
  • NaN == 0 is false.
{} == 0 // false

• Both sides are objects.
  • JavaScript compares object references.
  • Each object or array is a separate object.
  • Different object references return false.
{} == {} // false
[] == {} // false

• An array is truthy.
  • ![] becomes false.
  • JavaScript compares [] == false.
  • false becomes 0.
  • [] becomes "".
  • "" becomes 0.
  • JavaScript compares 0 == 0.
[] == ![] // true

column1: What do truthy and falsy mean?
column2:
• Truthy values act like true in a condition.
  • Falsy values act like false in a condition.
  • Arrays and objects are truthy.
  • ! reverses a truthy or falsy value.
Boolean([]) // true
Boolean({}) // true
Boolean("") // false
Boolean(0) // false

![] // false
